questions.question: What does one share of an ETF give you?
options: A small slice of a whole basket of companies
questions.explain: An ETF holds many stocks; one share owns a little of all of them.

questions.question: Tech stocks fall 8% and tech is 35% of MIX6. Roughly how much does MIX6 fall, if nothing else moves?
questions.explain: 35% × 8% ≈ 2.8%. The other 65% of the fund cushions the blow.

questions.question: Which portfolio is most diversified?
questions.explain: MKT100 holds 100 companies across 10 sectors. Three tech stocks are still one kind of risk.

questions.question: A stock has a beta of 1.6. The whole market falls 5%. What usually happens to the stock?
questions.explain: Beta 1.6 means it tends to move 1.6× the market: 1.6 × 5% = 8%.

questions.question: Your portfolio went $10,000 → $12,000 → $9,000. What is the maximum drawdown?
You lose 20%. What gain do you need to get back to where you started?
questions.explain: $10,000 → $8,000. Getting back to $10,000 needs +$2,000 on $8,000 = 25%. Losses hurt more than equal gains help.

questions.question: What is a bear market?
options: A market only for big investors
Prices down 20% or more from a peak
questions.explain: A fall of 20% or more from the last high, usually with fear and bigger swings.

questions.question: What does 'volatility clustering' mean?
options: Stocks in one sector move together
Big price swings tend to be followed by more big swings
Prices always return to their average
Volatility is the same every day
questions.explain: Calm follows calm and storms follow storms: after a shock, markets stay nervous for a while.

questions.question: Headline: 'Walmart sales not as bad as feared'. Good or bad news for Walmart's price?
questions.explain: Prices move on surprises. Better than feared is good news, even though a word counter says otherwise.

questions.question: You make 40 trades with a $1 fee each. What do you know for certain?
options: You paid $40 that you can't get back
questions.explain: Prices are uncertain but fees are guaranteed. Fewer, better decisions cost less.

questions.question: Dollar-cost averaging means…
options: Investing a fixed amount on a regular schedule
questions.explain: A steady schedule removes the stress of picking the perfect day and avoids putting everything in at the top.

questions.question: The Robo-analyst predicts next week's price correctly about 53% of the time. What's the best way to read that?
options: It's close to a coin flip: short-term prices are mostly unpredictable
You should trade every day on it
questions.explain: A small edge disappears after fees and bad luck. Even real professionals struggle to predict next week.

questions.question: Why does TradeSim test its ML model on markets it never trained on?
options: To catch overfitting and get an honest score
questions.explain: A model can memorise its training data. Only new data shows whether it learned a real pattern.

questions.question: In a sudden market-wide crash, which helps most?
options: Holding some cash or calmer, defensive assets
Buying the stock that fell most
Owning more stocks from the same sector
questions.explain: When everything falls together, diversification across stocks helps less; cash and defensive assets soften the blow.

questions.question: Your NVDA position is up $500 but you haven't sold. That $500 is…
questions.explain: It only becomes realised when you sell; tomorrow it could be bigger or smaller.

questions.question: Over long periods, most professional stock-picking funds…
options: Fail to beat a simple index fund
questions.explain: Studies such as S&P's SPIVA reports find most active funds trail their index over 10+ years, largely because of fees.

questions.question: You have $10,000 and use 2× leverage. Your shares fall 10%. What happens to YOUR money?
options: Nothing, the broker takes the loss
questions.explain: You hold $20,000 of shares; a 10% fall is $2,000, which is 20% of your own $10,000. Leverage multiplies losses as well as gains.

questions.question: What is a margin call?
options: The broker selling your shares because your own money fell too low
A phone call to buy more
questions.explain: When your equity drops below the maintenance level, the broker sells holdings to shrink the loan — usually right after a fall.

questions.question: At 5× leverage, roughly what fall in your holdings wipes out all of your own money?
questions.explain: Holdings are 5× your money, so a 20% fall equals 100% of your money. Wipe-out = 1 ÷ leverage.

questions.question: A 2× daily-reset fund goes up 10% then down 10% while the market goes +5% then −5%. Why is it behind 2× the market's result?
options: Volatility decay: resetting daily loses in zig-zags
questions.explain: Market: 1.05 × 0.95 = −0.25%. Fund: 1.10 × 0.90 = −1%, which is worse than 2 × −0.25%. The more prices zig-zag, the bigger the gap.

questions.question: On a price board, what does a yellow price usually mean?
options: The price equals yesterday's close (the reference)
questions.explain: Green is above the reference price, red is below, and yellow is unchanged.
